blocks.text: A tool name and description tell a model what a tool is for, but they say nothing precise about how to actually call it. That precision lives in one field: inputSchema. It is the part of a tool description written in a strict, structured language rather than prose, and it is what lets a model go from a vague intention to a call a server can trust and execute. This lesson works through that schema in real depth.
1. Why inputSchema Exists

blocks.alt: A model reads a schema, builds a call, and the server validates it

blocks.text: Without a schema, a model calling a tool would be guessing at argument names and shapes from the description alone, the same way a developer might guess at an undocumented function's parameters. Guessing works often enough to be dangerous, and fails silently or loudly in exactly the cases that matter most, like a required field being skipped or a date sent as the wrong kind of string.

inputSchema removes the guessing. It states, in a format both the model and the server can parse unambiguously, precisely which fields exist, what type each one must be, and which ones cannot be left out. A model that respects the schema and a server that validates against it are speaking the same exact language about what a valid call looks like.

blocks.title: The core idea
blocks.content: inputSchema turns a tool from a mystery box into something a model can inspect and reason about before ever calling it.

blocks.text: 2. JSON Schema in One Page

MCP uses JSON Schema, an existing, widely adopted standard for describing the shape of JSON data, rather than inventing its own format. This is a deliberate choice, it means every JSON Schema validator, code generator, and reference a developer already knows works directly with MCP tool schemas, nothing MCP-specific needs to be learned just to read one.

At its core, JSON Schema describes a value by stating its type, and if that type is an object, by describing each of its properties recursively the same way. Every inputSchema in MCP is, at the top level, an object schema, because tool arguments are always passed as a single JSON object of named fields, never as a bare list or a bare scalar.
3. The type Field

Every schema, and every property inside it, declares a type: string, number, integer, boolean, object, array, or null. This single field is doing more work than it looks like, it is the first and most basic check a value must pass before anything else about it is considered.

blocks.content: {"headers":["type","Example valid value","Notes"],"rows":[["string","\"Paris\"","Any JSON string"],["integer","3","Whole numbers only, no decimal point"],["number","3.5","Integers and decimals both"],["boolean","true","Exactly true or false"],["array","[\"a\", \"b\"]","An ordered list, usually with an items schema"],["object","{\"x\": 1}","A nested set of named properties"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Describing an Object: properties and required

blocks.alt: Properties and a required list together describe an object

blocks.text: An object schema has a properties field, mapping each field name to its own schema, and a required array, listing which of those property names must be present for the object to be considered valid. Any property not listed in required is optional, the caller may omit it entirely.
In this example, a call missing to or subject is invalid, but a call missing cc is perfectly fine, cc is simply left out of the arguments object entirely when not needed.
5. Required vs Optional in Practice

blocks.alt: A required field is compared against an optional field

blocks.text: Marking a field required is a strong statement, it tells every caller, and every validator, that a call without it is not just incomplete but outright invalid, and should be rejected before any tool logic even runs. Marking a field optional is not the same as saying it is unimportant, it usually just means the tool has a sensible fallback behavior when that field is absent.

items: Required: the tool genuinely cannot do its job without this value, like a recipient address for an email
Optional with a sensible default: the tool can proceed reasonably without it, like an email's cc field defaulting to none
Optional with no good default: often a sign the field should actually be required instead

blocks.text: 6. Expressing Defaults

JSON Schema supports a default keyword on a property, documenting what value the tool assumes when that optional field is left out. This does not mean the server automatically inserts that value into the arguments object, the model still simply omits the field, the default keyword is purely informative, telling the model, and any human reading the schema, what will happen if it is skipped.

A sensible default reduces how much a model needs to specify explicitly, but it should never be relied upon for anything security sensitive, a server should still validate every value it actually receives.
7. Arrays: Lists of a Single Shape

blocks.alt: An array field holds a list of items all sharing one shape

blocks.text: An array-typed field represents an ordered list, and its items keyword describes the schema every element in that list must satisfy. A tool that adds several tags to a note at once, for example, would take a tags field typed as an array of strings.

Arrays can also hold objects rather than plain scalars, which is how a tool represents something like a list of line items on an order, each one itself a small structured object with its own properties and required fields.
An array field always describes the shape of its items once, every element in the array is expected to match that same shape.
8. Enums: Constraining a Value to a Fixed Set

blocks.alt: An enum constrains a value to one of a fixed set of options

blocks.text: The enum keyword restricts a field to a specific, closed list of allowed values, rather than accepting any string or number. This is one of the most useful tools a schema author has, because it eliminates an entire category of invalid input before it ever reaches the server's own logic.

Without this enum, a model might reasonably send "urgent" or "High" for a priority field, values a human would understand but that the underlying system was never built to handle. With the enum in place, the model is steered toward exactly the three values the server actually supports.
9. Nested Objects

A property can itself be typed as an object, with its own nested properties and required array, letting a schema describe genuinely structured input, like an address embedded inside a larger shipping tool call, rather than flattening everything into top-level fields.

Nesting should be used with restraint. It is genuinely useful for grouping fields that belong together conceptually, like an address, but excessive nesting several layers deep makes a schema harder for a model to reliably fill in correctly, and harder for a human to review.
10. Per-Field Descriptions

Beyond type, required, and enum, every individual property can carry its own description string, explaining exactly what that one field means, its expected format, or any constraint the type system alone cannot express, like "must be a future date" or "in the user's local timezone."

These per-field descriptions matter just as much as the tool-level description discussed in the previous lesson, and are frequently under-written for the same reason, it is easy to assume a field name like due_date is self-explanatory when in practice the exact format and timezone assumption is not.
A short, specific description on each field, not just the tool overall, meaningfully improves how reliably a model fills in the right value for that field.
11. Beyond the Basics: Common Extra Keywords
JSON Schema supports a number of additional keywords that tighten validation beyond bare type checking. A few show up often enough in real MCP tool schemas to be worth knowing by name.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Keyword","Applies to","What it does"],"rows":[["minimum / maximum","number, integer","Bounds the numeric range of a valid value"],["minLength / maxLength","string","Bounds how many characters a string may have"],["pattern","string","Requires the value to match a regular expression"],["format","string","Hints at a semantic format, like date-time or email"],["minItems / maxItems","array","Bounds how many elements the array may contain"]]}

blocks.text: Keywords like minimum, maximum, and pattern let a schema constrain a value more precisely than type alone, catching an invalid call before it ever reaches the tool handler.
12. How a Model Actually Uses a Schema

When a model decides to call a tool, it is effectively performing a small act of structured generation: reading the schema, then producing a JSON object that satisfies it, field by field, using the surrounding conversation to decide what value belongs in each slot.

A required string field gets filled from whatever the user said that maps to it, an enum field gets mapped to the closest matching allowed value, an optional field gets included only if the conversation actually supplied something for it.

The clearer and more specific a schema description is, the more reliably a model constructs a valid, sensible call on the first attempt, vague descriptions lead to more retries and more validation failures.
13. Validation Is Enforced by the Server, Not the Model

blocks.alt: The server enforces validation rather than the model

blocks.text: A model doing its best to follow a schema is not a safety guarantee, models can still send a malformed call, whether from a misunderstanding, a typo, or an edge case the schema did not anticipate clearly enough. This is why a well-built server validates every incoming tools/call argument object against its own inputSchema before running any actual logic, rather than trusting that the model got it right.

blocks.title: The rule to remember
blocks.content: A schema describes what a valid call looks like, it does not enforce anything by itself. Enforcement is the server's job, performed at the moment a call arrives, before any side effect happens.

blocks.text: A model can propose an invalid call, the server is always the final authority on whether that call is actually acceptable, never assume client side or model side validation alone is sufficient.
14. What Happens When Validation Fails

blocks.alt: Failed validation returns an error rather than executing the tool

blocks.text: When an incoming call does not match the schema, a well-behaved server rejects it before executing anything, and reports back a clear, specific error rather than a generic failure. Which field was wrong, and why, is exactly the information a model needs to correct its next attempt.

A later lesson in this module covers error handling in full depth, but it is worth flagging here because schema validation failures are, in practice, one of the single most common categories of tool error a real system will encounter.
15. A Full Realistic Schema Walkthrough

Bringing every piece together, here is a complete, realistic inputSchema for a tool that books a restaurant reservation, using object nesting, an enum, an array, and a mix of required and optional fields all at once.

Reading this schema top to bottom tells a complete story: a reservation always needs a restaurant, a party size within a sane range, and contact details, while seating preference and dietary notes are nice-to-haves the tool can happily proceed without.

blocks.title: A design tip
blocks.content: Writing a schema is a lot like writing a function signature for a colleague who has never seen your codebase, be explicit, name things clearly, and do not assume shared context.

blocks.text: Worked Example

A user says: "Book us a table for 4 outdoors at the place on Main Street, my number is 555-0148, name is Priya, and one of us is vegetarian." Walking through the schema above field by field, the model has everything it needs to build a fully valid call.

Notice that every field maps directly back to something the user actually said, the model is not inventing values, it is translating natural language into the exact shape the schema demands, using the schema as a checklist of what still needs to be filled in.
Common Mistakes

items: Marking a field required when the tool actually has a perfectly good default, forcing every caller to specify something that rarely varies.
Leaving a field optional with no real default behavior defined anywhere, so the server has to guess what to do when it is missing.
Using a free-form string where an enum would eliminate an entire class of invalid values, like a status field that should only ever be one of three known states.
Writing a schema with correct types but no descriptions, leaving format assumptions like date formats or units completely unstated.
Nesting objects many layers deep for the sake of tidy organization, at the cost of making the schema harder for a model to reliably fill in.
Trusting that a model-generated call already matches the schema and skipping server-side validation before running tool logic.

blocks.text: A schema with vague field names like value1 and value2 forces a model to guess at meaning, specific names like departure_city communicate intent directly and reduce mistaken calls.
Practice

Write a complete inputSchema for a tool called update_subscription_plan, which changes a user's subscription tier. It should require a plan name constrained to a fixed set of allowed tiers, and accept an optional flag for whether to prorate the charge immediately. Include a description on every field.
Key Takeaway

inputSchema is standard JSON Schema describing a tool's arguments as an object with typed, optionally required properties, and it is what allows a model to go from a vague natural-language intention to a precisely shaped, checkable call. Types, required fields, enums, and nested objects each remove a different kind of ambiguity, and the server, never the model, is what ultimately enforces that the schema was actually followed.

With schemas covered in depth, the next lesson turns to the step that happens before any of this, tool discovery, the tools/list method a client uses to learn which tools, with which schemas, a server actually offers in the first place.
